name: English - The Science of Science Fiction C1
description:
Can members of a society without a tradition of science fiction make revolutionary scientific discoveries and produce game-changing technological developments? It is, of course, a provocative question. However, one issue I would like us to consider in this seminar is the relationship between thinking outside the box and being able to bring that thought to bear on the physical world and also be aware of the ethical consequences of our actions.

Starting with Jules Verne, and even Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein, authors have used the medium of fiction as a vehicle to speculate on the possibilities of science and technology and to imagine its potential for helping human beings as well as harming them. This ability to think beyond current knowledge and capability and to consider its implications for human life is certainly as important today as ever, on one hand as fuel to propel further growth and on the other hand to help to steer and guide it. 

In this colloquium-style seminar, we will select various works of popular science fiction literature and film to consider which scientific and social issues the works address, how accurate or plausible the predictions are, and evaluate these works for our own use. Authors will include Philip K. Dick, William Gibson, Neal Stephenson, Kim Stanley Robinson and Iain Banks.

You will also be able to view entire films of speculative fiction related to our topics in the parallel course English Through Cinema!
prerequisites: This course requires a large amount of reading, speaking as well as listening and writing at the C1 level. Therefore it is recommended for students who scored at least 60 percent on the English placement test. Exceptions can be made in the case of exceptionally motivated students.
